query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, the cyclic mechanical removal of a protective oxide film from the softer regions and interphase boundaries leads to exposure of adjacent phases with mismatched corrosion potentials. This in turn creates localized galvanic cells that accelerate anodic dissolution, so that wear and corrosion act synergistically to produce a degradation rate that is significantly higher than the sum of the individual effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a fine lamellar (e.g., alternating soft FCC and hard B2) microstructure that initially forms a continuous protective oxide film at ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Expose matched specimens to simultaneous wear and corrosion under elevated temperature versus a control where the alloy is subjected only to the same corrosion environment without significant mechanical wear (e.g., by reducing the applied load or using static immersion).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature conditions and a corrosive environment (such as a chloride-containing acidic solution) with a defined sliding wear test (specified load, sliding speed, and frequency) for the intervention, versus identical temperature and corrosive conditions without imposed wear for the control.
generation.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries of the lamellar eutectic microstructure and the integrity of the protective oxide film covering them.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear preferentially removes the relatively fragile oxide layer from the softer phase regions and especially at the interfaces between dissimilar phases. This exposure creates localized sites with different electrochemical potentials, triggering microgalvanic corrosion that further undermines oxide reformation. The cycle of oxide rupture and accelerated localized corrosion, coupled with continued abrasive wear, amplifies the overall degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline corrosion-only condition, the alloy undergoing simultaneous wear and corrosion will show a higher overall degradation with increased wear depth and more pronounced localized pitting (corrosion) at the interphase boundaries.
generation.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy test specimens exposed solely to the corrosive environment at the same elevated temperature but with minimal mechanical wear.
generation.boundary: Experiments conducted under controlled elevated temperatures and corrosive conditions (e.g., a defined chloride-acid solution) with the same alloy composition and initial microstructure, and with clearly specified mechanical loading/wear parameters versus static exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative enhancement of degradation due to the coupled mechanism is not precisely known and may depend on subtle variations in oxide film properties and interphase adhesion; further studies are needed to precisely isolate the individual contributions of wear-induced oxide removal and galvanic corrosion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject one set to a combined wear-corrosion protocol using a reciprocating sliding wear test at an elevated temperature in a corrosive solution, while exposing the other set to the corrosive solution under static or nearly zero-wear conditions. Additionally, vary the quality of the oxide film via a pre-treatment step to modify initial oxide adhesion. Compare the spatial distribution of corrosion pits, overall mass loss, and wear depth via microscopy and electrochemical measurements.
measurements: Corrosion pit density, size, and distribution (with emphasis on interphase boundaries)
Electrochemical impedance spectra indicating oxide film integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion do not exhibit significantly higher combined degradation (e.g., greater wear depth and enhanced localized pitting at phase boundaries) relative to the corrosion-only control, or if corrosion does not preferentially initiate at the interphase boundaries, then the hypothesis that wear-induced oxide film removal drives the accelerated coupled degradation should be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5.Keywords: high-entropy alloy (HEA), compositionally complex alloy (CCA), spark plasma sinterin

Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.
